title: Russian state stakes → loans-for-shares banks
summary: In 1995 the Russian government pledged tranches of shares in 12 large state companies, including Norilsk Nickel, Yukos, Sibneft, LUKoil and Surgutneftegaz, to private lenders at auctions, in return for loans to the federal budget totalling about $800 million. The government did not repay by the September 1996 deadline, so the lenders sold the stakes, usually to themselves. The auctions were often organised by banks linked to the winners. An English court later found that the Sibneft winner had no genuine competition.

private.outcome: The date above is the first auction, Norilsk Nickel's, in November 1995. The lenders took full ownership after the government failed to repay. Treisman's estimates: winners paid 13% (Norilsk), 16% (Sibneft) and 45% (Yukos) below late-1995 market valuations, and the biggest discounts went to the managers of LUKoil and Surgutneftegaz. Between end-1996 and end-2003 Sibneft's market capitalisation rose more than 10 times and Yukos' more than 50 times in dollar terms, against about three times for the RTS index.

links.claim: A London High Court judgment records that NFK, with Stolichny Savings Bank, won the Sibneft loans-for-shares auction on 28 December 1995 with a $100.3 million loan bid; NFK 'had no genuine competition', as other bidders were persuaded not to bid or to bid less, and Menatep's under-bid was pre-arranged.

links.claim: Peer-reviewed analysis: the state gave minority stakes in 12 large companies to lenders in return for loans of about $800 million; if not repaid by September 1996 the lenders could sell the stakes and keep 30% of any gain. The government did not repay, and the creditors sold the stakes, usually to themselves, at auctions with minimal competition.

links.claim: Uneximbank paid $170.1 million for its 38% bloc of Norilsk Nickel in the 1995 loans-for-shares transfer. On 5 August 1997 Svift, a company affiliated with Oneksimbank, won the auction for that stake with a bid of about $250 million.

sources.title: Russia: Privatization Of Norilsk Nickel Fuels Competition

links.claim: In December 1995 AOZT Laguna, backed by Bank Menatep, the bank that organised the auction, won 78% of Yukos in two combined auctions for $309.1 million. That included the 45% loans-for-shares stake, won with a $159 million bid against a $150 million minimum; the only rival bid was guaranteed by banks that also backed Laguna.

claims.claim: Oligarchs bought Russia's crown jewels for a tiny fraction of their value.
claims.explanation: The auctions were rigged in execution; a UK court found the Sibneft winner had no genuine competition. But Treisman estimates the oligarch winners paid 13–45% below late-1995 market prices for Norilsk, Sibneft and Yukos (28–53% at 1996 prices). The largest discounts, 69–89%, went to Soviet-era managers buying stakes in LUKoil and Surgutneftegaz.

claims.claim: Courts have ruled the loans-for-shares auctions illegal.
claims.explanation: The London High Court noted that Russia's Audit Chamber criticised the Sibneft auction in December 1997 (reserve too low, outcome fixed in advance) and found as fact that NFK had no genuine competition. It expressly declined to decide whether the auction was corrupt or unlawful under Russian law at the time.

claims.claim: Yukos, Norilsk Nickel and Sibneft were privatized via rigged voucher auctions designed by Harvard HIID advisors (Andrei Shleifer, Jonathan Hay) and USAID.
claims.explanation: The claim conflates two programs. The controlling stakes in Yukos, Norilsk Nickel and Sibneft changed hands in the 1995 loans-for-shares auctions documented in this record, not in the 1992-94 voucher auctions; the Sibneft stake was auctioned under a 1995 presidential decree as a loan-and-management deal (Court of Appeal, 2011), and this record's approved links show those auctions had minimal or no genuine competition. HIID's USAID-funded project did advise Anatoly Chubais's State Property Committee (GKI) on privatization (Institutional Investor; GAO 1995) and later worked on capital-market and legal reform (GAO 1996; the 2004 court opinion describes the project as assisting Russia in developing capital markets and foreign investments). No source found states that HIID, Shleifer, Hay or USAID designed the loans-for-shares auctions; Treisman's account attributes the bidding to Russian banks and their partners (Berezovsky sought Western partners for the Sibneft bid and found none). The U.S. case against Harvard, Shleifer and Hay concerned personal investments in Russia in breach of conflict-of-interest rules, not auction design. What is supported: the auctions were rigged in execution, and HIID advised the privatization agency; what is not: that the three companies went through voucher auctions, or that HIID advisers designed the auctions that transferred them.
